title: Building the box set and why Hammond mattered
summary: He pieced the concerts together over a long time, left out the tinny Victrola opening, and explains his class on Hammond integrating music before Jackie Robinson.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: electric guitar and then that would go on for a while and there would be a splice and here’s another solo from a totally different song. It was just solos on these reels, spliced together. And I started listening and it doesn’t take a genius to figure out that’s Lester Young trading off of Charlie Christian. These things. I get chill bumps as you can imagine. So I started — I was literally, I don’t know how many legal pads I filled with notes on this. And I got with Doug Sax and started constructing this stuff. By the end I had two sets of safeties made so I could keep one in Santa Monica and at Doug’s place in Hollywood, and also a set that I could take back to Nashville and be working on it in one of my other studios with other mastering engineers. And it took a long time as you can imagine, to piece this together. And I still couldn’t put it all in the box set. The box set is the best of the two concerts by far. Some of it was — I mean it was John Hammond with an old Victrola on the stage on a stool playing some old records. I mean this is in Carnegie Hall and they had a microphone with him playing a Victrola. Because I talked to Mr. Hammond about this at one time, before I even got the work up, because he was talking about all that stuff. So I remembered all that. But that was on the tapes but as you can imagine playing these old 78s on a Victrola on a stage at Carnegie Hall with a microphone. It was terrible, tinny and almost inaudible. But that’s how he would start the concert. And I just thought well that’s historically valuable. The tapes are certainly still in existence but I thought that’s not going to work for the CD box set. So anyway, it was an extensive undertaking but it was a labor of love. And I did know the music. And I knew Mr. Hammond, like I was talking about. You weren’t there this morning when I was talking about John Hammond. Because when I do my classes, “Rhythm & Blues Tore Down the Walls of Segregation,” my first class is about John Hammond, how he talked Benny Goodman into hiring Teddy Wilson and integrated music in 1935. And Lionel Hampton and Charlie Christian. And I talk to my student about this is twelve years before Jackie Robinson and the Dodgers. And that’s my whole basis of my class is music played the bigger part of integrating society than the courts or baseball or something like that. So I knew Mr. Hammond, I knew the music, and I was confident I could do it.
